title: Arcades: Nostalgia Abounds
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the history of the arcade, from the early days of Nolan Bushnell, Atari, and Pong in the early 1970s through the Golden Age of arcade video games (roughly 1978 to 1982) and iconic games like Space Invaders, Pac-Man, Asteroids, Donkey Kong, and Centipede. They cover tokens versus quarters, kill screens and high score tables, and the decline of arcades in the mid-1980s due to flooded markets of bad games, cultural backlash (including the 1982 Surgeon General C. Everett Koop remark and PTA report), and the rise of home consoles. They touch on a brief early-1990s revival with Street Fighter II and Mortal Kombat, and modern options like Dave & Buster's and barcades. The episode ends with a tour announcement at the start and listener mail with recipe and cooking tips at the end.

segments.title: Tour announcement
segments.summary: Hosts announce a Northeastern spring 2023 tour with dates in DC, Boston, and Toronto, and direct listeners to the ticket link.

segments.title: Introduction and early history of arcades
segments.summary: Hosts introduce arcades, the connection to pinball, and Nolan Bushnell's background as an engineer and amusement park games director, leading to the founding of Atari and its first game, Computer Space.

segments.title: Pong and the rise of coin-operated video games
segments.summary: Pong is introduced as a Tennis for Two descendant and a hit placed in a Sunnyvale bar, with about 35,000 cabinets sold, and Atari is sold to Warner Communications for about 28 million dollars.

segments.title: The Golden Age and arcade boom
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Golden Age of arcades from about 1978 to 1982 and the explosion to around 13,000 arcades in the US by 1982, along with the hosts' own childhood memories of local arcades.

segments.title: Latchkey kids and tokens versus quarters
segments.summary: The hosts discuss unsupervised kids in the arcade era and how early arcades used tokens with deals rather than quarters, contrasting this with modern Dave & Buster's style play.

segments.title: Iconic arcade games and their gameplay
segments.summary: The hosts discuss classic games that still hold up, such as Space Invaders, Galaga, Pac-Man, Centipede, Asteroids, Defender, and Tron, while noting Pole Position as dated, and Space Invaders' role in spawning shooter games.

segments.title: Pac-Man, Donkey Kong, and game trivia
segments.summary: The hosts cover Pac-Man's mascot design and the Pacman Fever record, Donkey Kong's name origin and Mario's original name Jumpman, Dragon's Lair as a LaserDisc game with weak gameplay, and other games such as Comanche, Empire City, Spy Hunter, and Battle Zone.

segments.title: Kill screens, high scores, and ports
segments.summary: The hosts explain kill screens caused by eight-bit processor limits in Pac-Man and Donkey Kong, the history of high score tables starting with Seawolf and Asteroids, and how arcade games looked better than home ports like Atari's Pac-Man.

segments.title: What killed the arcade
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the arcade decline: flooded markets of bad games, owners borrowing money for duds, the 1982 Surgeon General Koop remark and PTA report, the moral panic, and home consoles that parents tolerated over arcades.

segments.title: Early 1990s revival and modern barcades
segments.summary: The hosts note a brief early-1990s revival led by Street Fighter II, Mortal Kombat, and Tekken, the hosts' own memories of Mountasia and Chuck E. Cheese, and the modern rise of barcades.

segments.title: Listener mail: hamburger steak and kitchen tips
segments.summary: A listener named Lorie shares a meatloaf-style hamburger steak recipe with onion soup mix, and the hosts share a tip about reusing starchy pasta water in sauce and mashed potatoes, plus a note about salted butter preventing mold in butter bells.
